entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — A calendar will not add up
entries.cue: The world's hours and dates contradict one another.
entries.text: Papa, there is nothing wrong with a world keeping strange hours. There is something wrong with the same hour changing length whenever the plot requires it. Fix the units, then let us prove the calendar against a full year.

entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — A calendar will not add up
entries.cue: The world's hours and dates contradict one another.
entries.text: A calendar becomes believable when its conversions are consistent. Just so I understand: which unit is fixed, and which is only approximate?

entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — A calendar will not add up
entries.cue: The world's hours and dates contradict one another.
entries.text: I see. The central point, as I see it, is this: a calendar becomes believable when its conversions are consistent. Define the base units and test one complete year numerically. We ought to be satisfied only when this holds: the same date should convert identically wherever it appears. A measured approach will suit us better than a heroic guess.

entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — A language changes without rules
entries.cue: The invented language has lovely sounds but inconsistent evolution.
entries.text: An old tongue ought to carry marks of its own history. Let a few sounds change for clear reasons across generations, and the words will begin to look like relatives rather than strangers in matching costumes.

entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — A language changes without rules
entries.cue: The invented language has lovely sounds but inconsistent evolution.
entries.text: There is the point. What I notice first is this: a language gains history through regular sound changes and exceptions with causes. For a start, write a small timeline for the sounds before adding more vocabulary. I shall be persuaded when this is true: related words should show recognizable family resemblance.

entries.topic: Work / Worldbuilding — History reads like a textbook
